{"id": "eed19d92-1631-41b1-8100-349d7e05bda6", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_Zl1fjeXBBzY9WfwBsUEnLC", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"Amazon VPC FAQs\",\"context\":\"### What IP address ranges are assigned to a default Amazon VPC?\\n\\nDefault VPCs are assigned a CIDR range of 172.31.0.0/16. Default subnets within a default VPC are assigned /20 netblocks within the VPC CIDR range\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/vpc/faqs/\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Default VPC components\",\"context\":\"# Default VPC components\\n\\nWhen we create a default VPC, we do the following to set it up for you:\\n\\n* Create a VPC with a size `/16` IPv4 CIDR block (`172.31.0.0/16`).\\n This provides up to 65,536 private IPv4 addresses.\\n* Create a size `/20` default subnet in each Availability Zone. This provides up\\n to 4,096 addresses per subnet, a few of which are reserved for our use.\\n* Create an internet gateway and connect it to\\n your default VPC.\\n* Add a route to the main route table that points all traffic\\n (`0.0.0.0/0`) to the internet gateway.\\n* Create a default security group and associate it with your default VPC.\\n* Create a default network access control list (ACL) and associate it with your\\n default VPC.\\n* Associate the default DHCP options set for your AWS account with your default\\n VPC.\\n\\n**Note:**\\n\\n* Amazon creates the above resources on your behalf. IAM policies do not apply to these actions\\n because you do not perform these actions. For example, if you have an IAM\\n policy that denies the ability to call CreateInternetGateway, and then you\\n call CreateDefaultVpc, the internet gateway in the default VPC is still\\n created. To prevent Amazon from creating an internet gateway, you would have\\n to deny CreateDefaultVpc and CreateInternetGateway.\\n* To block all traffic to and from the internet gateways in your account, see Block public access to VPCs and subnets.\\n\\nThe following figure illustrates the key components that we set up for a default VPC.\\n\\nThe following table shows the routes in the main route table for the default VPC.\\n\\n| Destination | Target |\\n| --- | --- |\\n| 172.31.0.0/16 | local |\\n| 0.0.0.0/0 | `internet_gateway_id` |\\n\\nYou can use a default VPC as you would use any other VPC:\\n\\n* Add additional nondefault subnets.\\n* Modify the main route table.\\n* Add additional route tables.\\n* Associate additional security groups.\\n* Update the rules of the default security group.\\n* Add AWS Site-to-Site VPN connections.\\n* Add more IPv4 CIDR blocks.\\n* Access VPCs in a remote Region by using a Direct\\n\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/default-vpc-components.html\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"What Startups Should Know about Amazon VPC: Part 2 | AWS Startups Blog\",\"context\":\"### **AWS Regions**\\n\\nThe second step is to define a master IP CIDR block. All future subnets for this VPC will inherit the first two octets of the IP CIDR block that you define.\\n\\nOnce defined, the IP CIDR block is irreversible. It determines the number of subnets and IP addresses that you can create inside your VPC. Therefore, it is important that you chose a CIDR block that allows you to scale according to your needs today and in the future.\\n\\nYou can chose a CIDR block that is as small as a /28 or as large as a /16. A /28 will provide you with 16 IP addresses and a /16 will provide you with 65,536 IP addresses.\\n\\nThe following illustration shows a CIDR block relationship to VPC subnets.\\n\\nThe following screenshot shows how to create a CIDR block in the Amazon VPC console.\\n\\nAs shown in the screenshot, your private subnet should be the default for your resources unless they absolutely must have a public IP address attached to the instance. NAT instances are used to provide Internet access to your private subnet resources. You can use a bastian host to access them from a public domain such as the Internet. Note that you can access resources in the private subnet securely via a hardware VPN between your LAN and your VPC or via AWS Direct Connect\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/startups/what-startups-should-know-about-amazon-vpc-part-2/\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Verify the default VPC CIDR block claim in AWS documentation."}

{"id": "400e9c41-5950-41c9-918a-ebc3052be280", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Confirmed. Here's the breakdown:

- **Default VPC** (the one AWS auto-creates per region for your account): always gets a `/16` CIDR of **`172.31.0.0/16`**, giving ~65,536 private IPv4 addresses. Within it, each Availability Zone gets a default `/20` subnet (4,096 addresses each).
- **Custom VPC** (one you create yourself): there's no auto-assigned default — you must specify the CIDR block at creation time, choosing anywhere from a `/28` (16 addresses) up to a `/16` (65,536 addresses).

So if you're asking about the auto-generated default VPC, it's `172.31.0.0/16`. If you're creating a new VPC yourself, you'll need to pick the range.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
